title: Measurement Conversions Grade 4: The One Rule That Fixes Them All + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master measurement conversions for Grade 4 with one simple rule for length, mass, capacity and time, plus a free 8-question quiz and printable worksheet.
excerpt: Most Grade 4 conversion mistakes come from one confusion: when to multiply and when to divide. Here is the single rule that clears it up for length, mass, capacity and time, with a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Grade 4 student to change 3 kilometres into metres and you will often get 0.003 or 300 instead of 3000. The maths is not hard — the child simply guessed whether to multiply or divide. That single guess is where nearly every error in measurement conversions for Grade 4 begins, and it is exactly the thing worth fixing first. Get the direction right and the rest is just careful arithmetic.

Here is the whole topic in one sentence: a bigger unit holds more, so it takes fewer of them; a smaller unit holds less, so it takes more of them. That is the idea behind the rule I teach on day one and repeat until it sticks.

The one rule for measurement conversions in Grade 4

When you go from a bigger unit to a smaller one, you multiply. When you go from a smaller unit to a bigger one, you divide. Metres to centimetres? Metres are bigger, so multiply. Grams to kilograms? Grams are smaller, so divide.

I ask children to sanity-check every answer with one question: ‘Did the number get bigger when it should have?’ Change 5 m to cm and you should end up with more than 5, not less. It sounds obvious, yet it catches the most common slip — multiplying and dividing the wrong way round — before it reaches the answer line.

The numbers you multiply or divide by

The metric system runs on tens, so the conversion factors are friendly: 10, 100, and 1000. There is no need to memorise dozens of facts. These are the ones Grade 4 uses across length, mass and capacity.

km → m× 1000bigger to smaller2 km = 2000 m
m → cm× 100bigger to smaller4 m = 400 cm
cm → mm× 10bigger to smaller7 cm = 70 mm
kg → g× 1000bigger to smaller3 kg = 3000 g
l → ml× 1000bigger to smaller2 l = 2000 ml
g → kg÷ 1000smaller to bigger5000 g = 5 kg
cm → m÷ 100smaller to bigger350 cm = 3.5 m

Why 1000, 100 and 10 keep coming back

A kilometre is a thousand metres, a metre is a hundred centimetres, and a centimetre is ten millimetres. Mass and capacity use the same thousand-step: a kilogram is a thousand grams, a litre a thousand millilitres. Once a child sees that the same three numbers do all the work, the topic shrinks from scary to routine.

Time is the odd one out

Time does not run on tens, so it needs its own set of numbers. This trips up children who assume everything is × 1000. The relationships to know are:

  • 1 hour = 60 minutes
  • 1 minute = 60 seconds
  • 1 hour = 3600 seconds
  • 1 day = 24 hours

The rule still holds — hours to minutes is bigger to smaller, so you multiply by 60; seconds to minutes is smaller to bigger, so you divide by 60. Only the factor changes.

Converting mixed units

Real questions rarely come in tidy whole units. A child measures a table as 2 m 45 cm and needs it all in centimetres. Break it into two steps: change the big unit, then add the leftover. Convert the 2 m to 200 cm, then add the 45 cm already sitting there. So 2 m 45 cm = 245 cm.

The same approach works for 1 kg 250 g (1000 g + 250 g = 1250 g) and 3 l 500 ml (3000 ml + 500 ml = 3500 ml). One honest caveat from the classroom: children love to convert the big part and then forget to add the small part. Make ‘convert, then add’ a two-word chant and the forgotten step disappears.

Adding and subtracting measures

Once units match, adding and subtracting measures is ordinary arithmetic. The trap is doing it before the units agree. To add 1 m 20 cm and 75 cm, first make both centimetres: 120 cm + 75 cm = 195 cm, which you can report back as 1 m 95 cm.

Subtraction works the same way. A jug holds 2 l and you pour out 650 ml — convert the 2 l to 2000 ml, then 2000 − 650 = 1350 ml. In my experience teaching nine-year-olds, the students who pause to line up units first almost never lose marks here; the ones who rush straight to the sum almost always do.

A quick practice routine that works

Ten focused minutes beats a marathon session. A pattern I recommend to parents in Tier-2 cities where tuition time is tight: one day on length, one on mass and capacity, one on time, and one on mixed units and adding measures. On the fifth day, mix them all so the child has to decide the factor and the direction without a hint. That deciding step is where true fluency shows.

Keep a ruler, a kitchen scale and a measuring jug within reach. A child who has actually poured 500 ml twice to make a litre understands × 1000 in a way no worksheet alone delivers — though the worksheet is where the practice locks in.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free eight-question quiz covering length, mass, capacity, time and mixed units — exactly the conversions above. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for any misses. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end offers graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Measurement Conversions Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on length, mass, capacity, time and mixed units. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: How many metres are in 3 kilometres?
questions.explanation: Kilometres are bigger than metres, so multiply. 3 × 1000 = 3000 m.
Centimetres are smaller than metres, so divide by 100. 500 ÷ 100 = 5 m.

questions.q: How many grams are in 4 kilograms?
questions.explanation: Kilograms are bigger, so multiply by 1000. 4 × 1000 = 4000 g.
Centimetres are bigger than millimetres, so multiply by 10. 7 × 10 = 70 mm.

questions.q: How many millilitres are in 2 litres?
questions.explanation: Litres are bigger, so multiply by 1000. 2 × 1000 = 2000 ml.

questions.q: How many seconds are in 2 minutes?
questions.explanation: Minutes are bigger than seconds, so multiply by 60. 2 × 60 = 120 s.
Convert 2 m to 200 cm, then add the 45 cm. 200 + 45 = 245 cm.

questions.q: Add 1 m 20 cm and 75 cm. What is the total in centimetres?
questions.explanation: Make units match: 1 m 20 cm = 120 cm. Then 120 + 75 = 195 cm.

faq.q: How do I know whether to multiply or divide in a conversion?
faq.a: Check which unit is bigger. Going from a bigger unit to a smaller one you multiply; going from a smaller unit to a bigger one you divide. A quick sanity check: the number should get larger when you move to a smaller unit.

faq.q: What conversion factors does a Grade 4 student need to know?
faq.a: For metric measures: ×10 for cm to mm, ×100 for m to cm, and ×1000 for km to m, kg to g and l to ml. For time: 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, and 24 hours in a day.

faq.q: Why is time harder than length or mass?
faq.a: Length, mass and capacity all run on tens, so the factors are 10, 100 or 1000. Time runs on 60 and 24 instead, so children must switch factors. The multiply-or-divide rule still works exactly the same.

faq.q: How do you convert mixed units like 2 m 45 cm?
faq.a: Convert the big unit first, then add the leftover. Change 2 m to 200 cm, then add the 45 cm to get 245 cm. The common slip is converting the big part and forgetting to add the small part.
